analysis_plan.ci: 95% paired percentile bootstrap over cases: 10000 resamples of case indices (random.Random(0), cases sorted by case_id), the same resamples for both skills, linearly interpolated quantiles
analysis_plan.descriptive: per-skill micro precision, recall and F1 and macro F1 with CIs; paired macro-F1, micro-precision and micro-recall differences; cost, completions, parse failures, violations
analysis_plan.design: paired: the baseline and the candidate skill each review the same sealed test cases once (sample 0), same model, provider, budget, prompt and parser; calls interleave per case, in case_id order the baseline goes first on the 1st, 3rd, ... case and the candidate on the 2nd, 4th, ...
analysis_plan.interpretation: the candidate counts as better on the sealed test only if the primary CI lower bound is above 0; the secondary result cannot override the primary; synthetic hand-written cases, so no claim of a real Hermes improvement
analysis_plan.missing_data: a call that errors or reports no cost is re-sent once automatically by the spend-ledger wrapper (as in the full run); a call still failed after that, skipped (cost cap) or unparseable is scored as an empty review for that skill and case; nothing else is re-run
analysis_plan.primary: candidate minus baseline micro-F1 under STRICT scoring (gate 3 verifier, exact normalised category)
analysis_plan.secondary: candidate minus baseline micro-F1 under LENIENT scoring (strict rules, plus the label audit's alternate categories)

headline: Pre-registered sealed final evaluation (run once, live Hermes, 10 hand-written synthetic test cases): candidate `github-code-review@28dcec5ab528` minus baseline `github-code-review@11ad06e6d49b`, STRICT micro-F1 +0.302 [0.157, 0.462] (primary; CI lower bound above 0, so the pre-registered rule is met), mostly precision (precision +0.446 [0.260, 0.600], recall +0.111 [0.000, 0.375]); LENIENT micro-F1 +0.332 [0.194, 0.474] (secondary).

Live full run live-1 (2-arm comparison on live Hermes outcomes, validation split): the best fixed strategy `fixed:skill` has utility 0.607; no adaptive policy improves on it: epsilon_greedy -0.032 [-0.039, -0.024] (worse); linucb -0.034 [-0.041, -0.026] (worse).

GEPA candidate `github-code-review@28dcec5ab528` (parent `github-code-review@11ad06e6d49b`) was admitted by gate 6 with a validation utility gain of +0.127 [+0.006, +0.272]; gate 7's post-admission check then kept it (catalogue validation utility 0.617 -> 0.809).

Simulator: No adaptive policy shows an improvement over the best fixed strategy (`fixed:structured`) on held-out validation: epsilon_greedy -0.006 [-0.024, +0.014] (no improvement detected); linucb +0.012 [-0.009, +0.033] (no improvement detected).

On train, epsilon_greedy +0.025 [+0.007, +0.043]; linucb +0.041 [+0.026, +0.056] against `fixed:structured`. That baseline was chosen in hindsight on the same train data, so this does not show generalisation.
Every adaptive policy beats uniform random selection in both phases.
A live Hermes smoke run scored 4 validation cases (4 completed, 0 violations). With so few cases this is a plumbing check, not a quality estimate.

The simulator findings are results from a hypothetical simulator, not from Hermes. The live full run (live-1), the one-time sealed final evaluation and a 4-case smoke test used live Hermes on a hand-written, synthetic benchmark, so none of this is evidence of real-world improvement.
